title: Downhill Sections Are Crucial for Performance in Trail Running Ultramarathons - A Pacing Strategy Analysis
authors: Genitrini M, Fritz J, Zimmermann G, Schwameder H
journal: Journal of Functional Morphology and Kinesiology
population: Public results from 16 races (4 courses, multiple editions); linear mixed model
findings: Better finishers ran downhill at higher relative speeds and uphill at lower relative speeds than slower finishers (p < 0.001).
In later race stages the relative speed drop was larger downhill than uphill (p < 0.001), for men and women.
Slower finishers lost the most downhill time in late stages (p < 0.001).
Among elite athletes no pacing difference between faster and slower finishers was found.
Elite women slowed more than men in late stages regardless of terrain (p < 0.001).
limitations: Race-website data from 4 courses (16 races) analysed with a linear mixed model of relative speed; no physiological, technicality or training-history data, and the number of athletes is not given in the abstract.
implications: Do not treat downhill as free time: relative speed fell more on descents than ascents in late race stages, for men and women, so apply a larger late-race slowdown to descents in an ultra pace model.

Better finishers ran downhill at higher and uphill at lower relative speeds than slower finishers. This is an association in observational data; it suggests, but does not show, that downhill durability separates finishers, so budget downhill-specific preparation for ultra goals.

verification.notes: Crossref: J Funct Morphol Kinesiol 7(4):103, 2022 (online 2022-11-21), four authors match. PubMed PMID 36412765 abstract supports all findings. Softened the causal wording in implications (observational).
